bridge: P04 introduced parsing and validation. This lesson uses fictional XML documents and an isolated parser exercise.
teaching:
### Read the structure first

XML describes nested elements and attributes. A parser turns that text into a structure the program can use. A well-formed document follows XML syntax; it can still contain values or features your application should not accept.

### Understand an external entity

Some XML configurations allow an entity to refer to content outside the document. Resolving it may read a local file or make a network request. Untrusted input should not be able to choose those reads merely because the application wanted to parse a document.

An XML external entity issue, often shortened to XXE, arises from unsafe use of those capabilities.

### Disable unnecessary capabilities

Use a maintained parser with settings appropriate to untrusted documents. Disable external entity resolution and related document features when they are not needed. Confirm the actual library and version defaults instead of assuming all XML parsers behave alike.

### Bound the work

A document can also demand excessive expansion, nesting or processing. Set input, depth and resource limits suitable for the application. Restrict the parser's filesystem and network authority as another layer.

Test allowed ordinary documents and specifically blocked capabilities using harmless local fixtures. A successful parse only tells you that the parser accepted the syntax, not that processing was safe.

### Read the validator and XML checklist

raw is input text. raw.encode("utf-8") produces its bytes so len can count them. isinstance(value, dict) checks for a dictionary; set(data) collects its distinct keys. != means not equal, so set(data)!={"body"} rejects any missing or extra key. Python’s or stops when the left side is true, so the shape expression does not try set(data) for a non-dictionary. str is the Python text type.

A DTD, or document type definition, can declare XML structure and entities. An external DTD lives outside the submitted document; fetching it can trigger file/network access. Depth means how many elements are nested inside one another. A schema describes allowed structure and values. For the parser-selection task, record these required capabilities/settings on paper; do not assume the JSON example is an XML parser or that its 200-byte limit proves every parser safe.
explanation: The byte limit is checked before parsing this small input. The shape rule rejects unknown fields rather than treating a field called url as an instruction to fetch it. JSON syntax alone does not ensure body has the expected type.
exercise: Test the supplied function with {"body":"demo"}, {"body":7}, {"body":"x","url":"https://example.org"}, [] and malformed text. Record which validation stage rejects each case.
solution:
Only the first input returns demo. To observe each rejection without stopping at the first exception, add this below the function and run the file again.

```python
cases = [
    '{"body":"demo"}',
    '{"body":7}',
    '{"body":"x","url":"https://example.org"}',
    '[]',
    'not JSON',
]
for raw in cases:
    try:
        print("accepted:", parse_note(raw))
    except ValueError as error:
        print("rejected:", type(error).__name__, str(error))
```

The second fails body type, the third extra-key shape, the fourth top-level shape, and the fifth JSON syntax. JSONDecodeError is a subclass of ValueError, so this harness catches it too. Nothing in this function interprets url as an instruction to fetch. The byte limit is an additional check, not a complete general resource-safety proof.
challenge: Write a parser selection checklist for accepting XML from an untrusted training source. Include external entities, external DTDs, network/file access, size/depth limits and schema validation. State why a code review must inspect the selected parser's actual settings.
challenge_solution: Capabilities/defaults differ across libraries and versions. The checklist must become concrete documented options and negative tests in the designated lab; merely naming XXE or relying on a filename does not establish safe parsing.
